utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning to the interpreters. Be sure that they can hear me. Also good morning to the Prosecution. Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Gentlemen, I would like to offer to you both my very sincere apologies for my tardiness in arriving this morning. I think I must have been misled by the usual rhythm of our proceedings of a Monday. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Judge Shahabuddeen. All of us run into some problems occasionally, and, of course, it's natural for everybody to apologise for what he is guilty of, but I'm particularly sensitive to the fact that Judge Shahabuddeen said what he just said. We can now proceed on the basis of the decision that was rendered on Friday. We are to hear the testimony of Vladimir-Djuro Degan, this morning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I want to thank you for the more detailed summary that you have given us today. I am sure you have told the professor what we talked about on Friday and about what questions could be asked. All right, I think we can agree to that. Do we agree with that Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We do. We have informed him, he has applied a scalpel to his notes and prepared comments to reduce and redact them, and I think he has done a serious job at that. If he errs in any respects, I'm sure, in any material respects, I'm sure we will hear and take appropriate steps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm sure that the Prosecutor also has a scalpel, I'm sure he does, and we too have our own scalpel. I think things should go without any hitches, but on the basis that was indicated here, all of us would be interested in hearing what the professor has to say in respect of the information that the Defence wants to give us. Here is the professor. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm very sensitive and pleased by this early greeting you are giving me. Before you sit down, please give us your name, your first name, what your position is, and then remain standing for a few more moments in order to take an oath and then you can sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Vladimir-Djuro Degan. I come from Zagreb, I now live in Croatia. I was born at Bosanski Brod which is now called Srpski Brod, according to the Dayton Agreements in the Republic of Srpska. I am a professor, I teach at the law school in Rijeka. I teach international public law, and I also direct an institute in Zagreb which is called the Adriatic Institute which deals with maritime law and the law of the sea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. If you would please remain standing for a moment and take the oath before the International Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor. You may be seated now. The Tribunal is very sensitive to your arrival at the request of the Defence in this trial initiated by the Prosecutor at International Criminal Tribunal of Colonel Blaskic, who is now a General, the accused, who is sitting in this courtroom to your left. In a decision taken by the Trial Chamber on Friday, we limited your remarks in order that they be focused on the points of fact, which are those of the trial that are of interest to us, and not a strictly legal perspective, since the Judges are qualified to deal with and to resolve legal questions that are raised before this Tribunal. There we go. If everything was explained to you, I think now, without any further ado, we should give the floor to Mr. Hayman. It is now a quarter to 11 and we will take a break in about an hour or hour and 15 minutes. Mr. Hayman, proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Hayman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor Degan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I would like to commence by handing out copies of the professor's curriculum vitae in French and English, perhaps it could be marked as one exhibit with an A and B subcomponent. Perhaps the French could be A and the English B.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, this document would be D468A for the French version, B for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, while your curriculum vitae is being handed out, let me ask you to speak more slowly than your natural rhythm of speech would be and we allow for a slight gap in our questions and answers for clarity of interpretation. Also, if I could ask the clerk to move the ELMO slightly. Thank you very much. Professor, we have distributed your curriculum vitae, could you, though, briefly describe your academic career and the academic positions you have held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I just told, I'm now teaching the public International Law at Rijeka University and I run an institute on maritime law and the law of the sea in Zagreb. I don't know whether you are interested in my education, which everything is written in my curriculum vitae.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In a few words, could you tell us what degree or degrees you hold, and the like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I took my doctor's degree at the University of Ljubljana. My thesis was on treaty interpretation, which I wrote originally in French and published here in the Hague, 1963, it's a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Welcome back to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you. And later on, I took Habilitation, that's a German system which was used in Croatia at the University of Zagreb. And I wrote another book in French, it's title is L'ecoute et le Droit International, or Equity in International Law, but equity in a different sense than common law equity. So I followed the courses at The Hague academy of International Law in eleven instances between 1960 -- 1959 until 1971, and I was twice the member of centre of studies and research here at The Hague Academy in the French section. I published articles and books in Croat, English and French. Last year was published here my big book in HE English language, Sources of International Law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Professor, on the second page of your curriculum vitae under nonjudicial legal activities, it indicates you've been a member of an expert group on state succession and a member of the Croatian delegation in negotiations on succession issues of the former Yugoslavia. Could you briefly describe your work in those capacities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. I took part since the beginning at the conference on the former Yugoslavia which started here in The Hague in 1991. I was the first Croatian member in the work and group on human rights and rights of minorities. Later on this conference started the negotiation process which did not end on state succession. It still lasts. But I must say that is an expert job, and in problems of state succession the positions of Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Slovenia and Macedonia are the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Vis-a-vis the Federal Republic or former --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The former Republic of Yugoslavia, which claims identity of continuity with the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which disappeared. In that respect, there are no differences in my actual job, which is an expert job with the views and positions of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me also ask you, at the end of your curriculum vitae you identify two decorations; could you describe those for the Court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was awarded by the French government for teaching International Law in the French language at French Universities, Le Mans, Nanterre, Pantheon-Assas and for teaching in French and organising French lectures and also English lectures at the Inter-University Centre of postgraduate studies in Dubrovnik. And I flatter myself that the French government awarded me also for my contribution of the doctrine of International Law in the French language, but perhaps it was a courtesy of that government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Defence has asked you to come here, and we thank you for coming, to address the Court on the subject of the formal state-to-state relations between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina at times relevant to this case and how those relations bear on the issue of the existence or nonexistence of an international armed conflict in Central Bosnia, the territory for which the accused in this case, General Blaskic, was the Operative Zone commander. Could you please provide the Court the information and comments that you have prepared on this subject?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I will start reading in the English language, but I have an accident, I have my arm broken. That accident happened in Zagreb, I was cured here in the Hague. I cannot take notes by my hand, but I think it will not prevent me in my job here today. Mr. President, Your Honour, the problem which I will discuss is the state-to-state relations of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, and there are consequences relating to whether General Blaskic can be accused for a commission of grave breaches of the 1949 Geneva Conventions under Article 2 of the Statute of this Tribunal. By that part of his indictment the Prosecutor alleges that in the period between May, 1992 and January, 1994 there was an international armed conflict in the valley of Lasva between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia. All four Geneva Conventions of 1949, except Common Article 3, apply in international armed conflicts. The appeals Chamber of this Tribunal noted in its decision of 2nd of October, 1995 in the Tadic case --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, excuse me Professor Degan. Mr. President, the decision of the Trial Chamber was to restrict Professor Degan to facts, not law and not comments on the decisions that have been rendered by this Tribunal; and therefore, I am offering an objection to his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Professor, the Trial Chamber's decision was very clear. We didn't expect you to give us an interpretation of the Geneva Conventions or for you to tell us whether General Blaskic should be prosecuted in respect of the indictment that was issued here. This is a decision of the Judges. I think you have to remain with the question that was asked by Mr. Hayman, that is: Were the former relations among the states, did they, rather, did they have any influence on the armed international conflict in your opinion? Your opinion on the interpretation of the Geneva Conventions is, of course, relevant, and with your curriculum vitae it is, of course, something which is important, but that is not what the Trial Chamber is asking for. The discussion took place on Friday and we circumscribed the questions which were be to taken up by you. You are here as an expert to speak about the relations between the states and their influence, in your opinion, of an international armed conflict. The Judges will then know at the proper time how to interpret the relevant provisions of the Geneva Conventions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I misled the witness, I apologise. I understood on the Court's ruling on Friday that he would be allowed to introduce his subject by painting a construct or a framework for the relevant facts, and that framework is necessarily a legal framework. So I understand that by mentioning the Tribunal or the Appellate Chamber the professor may have pushed a hot button for the Prosecutor, but I can represent to the Court that there is a framework that the professor would like to paint, and the bulk of his comments are relating to factual matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I don't want there to be an incident at each sentence, and that's why I've allowed myself to intervene the way I did. If we want to avoid frequent interruptions the witness might make his legal presentation introduction quickly but then move quickly to what was asked of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Professor, to do so. I know it's difficult to speak ad hoc on these types of issues, but please, as we have discussed and as the Court has directed, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm in a very unhappy position, because there is some confusion in interpretation of some parts of the four Geneva Conventions, and there are different doctrinal opinions, and I wanted to explain my opinion which are closely linked to the facts of General Blaskic. I can avoid all of that, but I think it would be a pity. I can just say that framework of that division of armed conflicts before 1949 and after 1949, but I think it will be useful to this Court. It would be different at the International Court of Justice, but if you don't allow me --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the Court is indicating that you will be allowed a brief period to paint the legal framework, keeping in mind that the bulk of your comments, will, as I believe you have planned and intended, will be factual.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Chairman, with your permission, I will quote the Tadic case in respect to four Geneva Conventions. It was said that in the present state of development of the law, Article 2 of the Statute only applies to offences committed within the context of international armed conflicts. My comment is that it cannot be otherwise, at least in criminal law. Grave breaches of conventions applicable to international armed conflicts apply only to this type of hostilities and not in noninternational armed conflicts, nor in situations of internal disturbances. My comment is also if the Prosecution fails to prove in the present proceedings that in the critical period and in the critical region of Bosnia-Herzegovina there was an international armed conflict of that stage, of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which Croatia -- my comment is that General Blaskic can be indicted only for violations of the laws or customs of war or for crimes against humanity, that is because Articles 3 and 5 of this Tribunal Statute apply to internal armed conflicts, as well. I don't know whether the Prosecution complies to this, my comment; if not, I will proceed. Now I would like to introduce the framework for this issue, which will be pointed out on factual, on facts which happened in relations between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina in the critical period between May 1992 and January 1994. Prior to the 1949 Geneva Conventions on humanitarian law, classical International Law knew only three types of armed conflicts; they were war, civil war and use of force short of war, such as armed reprisals, self-defence, other kinds of armed interventions, like Pacific blockade of a part of the coast of a foreign state, et cetera. Conventional rules which are now in force distinguish between international armed conflicts, armed conflicts not of an international character, or noninternational or internal armed conflicts, and finally, situations of internal disturbances and tensions which are not armed conflicts. However, as I already mentioned, this repetition did not avoid certain doctrinal confusions which I want to discuss here. In respect to the criteria for existence of all these three different situations, it is Common Article 2 of the four Geneva Conventions which gives criteria for existence of international armed conflicts. Those are all cases of declared wars that situation between high contracting parties, that is to say sovereign states, that these conventions equally apply to any other armed conflict which may arise between two or more states, even if the state of war is not recognised by one of them. That's my interpretation. I think it can be of some use in these trial proceedings, that this part of the phrase in Article 2, paragraph 1 of four Geneva Conventions means a contrario that there is no international armed conflict if all belligerent parties deny the existence of the state of war. In this respect exactly, most doctrinal writings neglect that difference. Probably in the light of the large after-war practice of denials of state of war. The third situation of international armed conflicts is provided in paragraph 2 of Article 2. It reads: "Conventions shall apply to all cases of partial or total occupation of the territory of a high contracting party, even if the said occupation meets with no resistance." Under the impact of later developments in general International Law, paragraph 4 of Article 1 of the 1977 Protocol I of the Geneva Conventions, assimilates into international armed conflicts some kinds of armed struggles which were previously considered as civil wars. Those are conflicts in which peoples are fighting against Colonial domination, and alien occupation or against racist regimes. However, no party --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Professor Degan. Excuse me, Mr. President and Judge Shahabuddeen, but again I hearken back to the ruling of this Chamber, which was that Professor Degan would come to discuss facts, and now he's giving us his interpretation and his point of view in respect of various Articles contained in the Geneva Conventions, and that is precisely what I thought the decision of the Chamber sought to avoid. A Chamber itself is fully capable of understanding and interpreting the law of the Geneva Conventions. In fact, that is the Chamber's mandate. So I would object, once again, Mr. President, and I would ask that Professor Degan get to the facts about which he intends to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Professor. I have to sustain that objection, and that was why, through the Defence counsel, to refer you in the French version to the summary that Mr. Hayman prepared on your testimony. Let me remind you of it, because apparently it has to be repeated, that most of the testimony will deal with the theoretical framework, which will allow us to answer the question of knowing whether in the period of interest there was an armed international conflict in Central Bosnia. The question is very simple; in your opinion, was there an armed international conflict or not? The second question was to describe the circumstances which allow us to conclude there was an international armed conflict according to the Geneva Conventions as indicated in Common Article 2. Nothing prevents your giving us your interpretation, but do it very quickly, please. The Judges will note it as evidence which has been tendered into the case file. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now I'll pass to the facts to make the Prosecution satisfied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We thank you very much for that. Well, we're not trying to please the Prosecution, you see, or to please the Judges. Each person simply has to do what he has to do in this Tribunal. It's not to please one party or the other. That's not why we're here. Please continue, but remain within the scope that we've indicated, and this is the last comment we can make on this point, otherwise, we have to redefine the scope of your intervention. If you agree, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In fact, what happened in the valley of Lasva from January 1993 to January 1994 was not of such a low intensity as to be qualified as internal disturbances or tensions against the central power of the state. That's the factual situation. For an international armed conflict to exist, it must be proven that one of the conflicting parties, namely Bosnia-Herzegovina or Croatia, formally declared war to another, or, alternatively, that any of them recognised the state of war, or, finally, that there was a final occupation of that faction of Bosnia-Herzegovina territory of the Croatian army according to the provisions on occupation which are still in force. They are led down in Articles 42 to 56 of the regulations respecting the Laws and Customs of War on Land in 1907. If it was not the case, there are still other criteria to be satisfied for the existence of international armed conflicts, which I shall discuss. I would like only to note here that use of force non-authorised by the Security Council or a crime of aggression can consist in single acts, then it does not necessarily create a state of war or a state of international armed conflict, because there is not a protracted armed conflict. As examples, I can point to the U.S. bombing of Libian territory for its involvement in terrorist acts in Berlin in 1986, or its launching of cruise missiles against installations used by terrorists in the Afganistan and Sudan of this year. Those are some facts that happened outside of Bosnia-Herzegovina and valley of Lasva. Regardless of the actual situation in the valley of Lasva, I want now to examine whether at any time between 1992 and 1995 there existed a state of war. That is to say, objective situation of an international armed conflict between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. I told already that neither of these two states declared war one to another, that's the fact, nor they recognised the state of war between themselves. I also said that there is no proof that Croatian army kept under occupation any part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Those are also facts with some legal qualifications. In this respect, the situation is sharply different with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. On 20th of June, 1992, Bosnia-Herzegovina proclaimed a state of war, identifying Serbia, Montenegro, the Yugoslav army and the local Serbian Democratic Party in Bosnia-Herzegovina as aggressors. From the state practice in wartime appeared some additional criteria for ascertainment of the existence of the state of war, which I want to examine now in four points. Point (A), the outbreak of a war has, as its immediate effect, rupture of diplomatic and consular relations between belligerent states. Nothing similar happened between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia. Embassies of two states, in Zagreb and Sarajevo respectively, exercised unimpeded all their functions since establishment of diplomatic relations near the end of 1992. I hope the Prosecution will not interrupt me now. I can give here some details collected from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Croatia. After the two states formally recognised one another as independent states on 7th of April, 1992, only a few days later on they agreed, on 14th of April, that their diplomatic and consular missions abroad will protect interests of nationals of the other state party where only one of them had such a mission. Pursuant to paragraph 9 in the Agreement of Friendship and Co-operation of 21st of July, 1992, on 25th of July, on next 25th July, they reached an agreement on establishment of diplomatic relations between two states. On 29th of September, Croatian president Tudjman accredited Mr. Zdravko Sancevic as first Croatian ambassador in Sarajevo. Mr. Sancevic delivered his letter of credence to President Itzebegovic in Sarajevo on 17th of November, 1992. Madam Bisera Turkovic was accredited by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina as its first ambassador in Croatia on 19th of January, 1993. She delivered her letter of credence to President Tudjman on following 25th of March. On 14th of June, 1993, President Tudjman was in official visit to besieged Sarajevo, in his effort to stop the conflict of HVO with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, in the period between January 1993 and January 1994, for which General Blaskic is accused for grave breaches of Geneva Conventions, Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina did not interrupt their diplomatic relations. In that very period, they established and developed them. However, because of the practice of some belligerents to keep diplomatic relations even during full-fledged hostilities, like China and Japan until 1st of February, 1938, the Soviet Union and Japan, during hostilities in Siberia and Mongolia in mid 1938 and in 1939, or Iran and Iraq throughout the war between 1980 and 1988, of importance are other tests of existence of an international armed conflict which I'll discuss now. Point (B), the outbreak of war has considerable effects on treaties between belligerent states. Not one treaty enforced between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia was suspended or abrogated, even in the period of hostilities between HVO and Bosnian army in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In this respect I would like to add that there are now not generally agreed rules on effects of international armed conflicts on multilateral and bilateral treaties of which belligerents are parties. That important topic remained outside the scope of the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, and I discussed that problem in my book on sources of International Law, pages 465 to 469, where I analysed a resolution on this subject matter adopted by l'Instiut de Droit International in 1985. However, from the former state practice it can be concluded the following: The first, the outbreak of war cancels all bilateral treaties on political or military co-operation or alliances between the belligerents. On this account, no party cancelled the above mentioned Agreement on Friendship and Co-operation of 21st of July, 1992. Second, during the wartime, each of belligerents is free to suspend the operation of treaties on trade, commerce and similar matters unless the U.N. Security Council decides otherwise. This relates, above all, to all bilateral treaties between belligerents, but not to multilateral treaties or treaties constituting international organisations of which all belligerents are parties. I examined, to this end, the situation of bilateral treaties between two states concerned before January 1993. In a list provided by the Croatian Foreign Ministry, besides the above-mentioned agreements on diplomatic representation abroad, on friendship and on establishment of diplomatic relations, I found only a protocol between two governments dating before the proclamation of independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The matter was of the Protocol of 27th of February, 1992 on co-operation in settlement of problems of refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina in Croatia. This means that in that tragic period of Serbian occupation of one-third of Croatian territory, with a huge number of Croatian displaced persons from its own occupied territories like Vukovar, Gospic and others, Croatia continued to receive refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Bilateral treaty relations expanded greatly after the Washington Framework Agreement on Confederal Relations of 18th of March, 1994. However, there is no evidence that either Bosnia-Herzegovina or Croatia cancelled or suspended the operation of any of the agreements I have mentioned. All of them were applied under the circumstances even after January 1993. Finally, the outbreak of hostilities renders operative multilateral and bilateral treaties which expressly provide to be operated during the armed conflicts. While the International Committee of the Red Cross was active to conclude ad hoc agreements on application of Geneva Conventions and protocols between Croatia and SFRY and the JNA in summer 1992, I have no data that these conventions on humanitarian law were applied any time in relations between Croatia on the one side and Bosnia-Herzegovina on the other. Point (C), the outbreak of hostilities has important effects on enemy citizens in the territory of another belligerent state. An important objective test of existence of an international armed conflict proceeds from Article 4, paragraph 2 of the 1949 Fourth Geneva Convention relative to the protection of civilian persons in time of war. With permission of the Prosecution, I'll quote it: "Nationals of a neutral state who find themselves in the territory of a belligerent state, and nationals of co-belligerent state shall not be regarded as protected persons while the state of which they are nationals has normal diplomatic representation in the state in whose hands they are." The fact is that no citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina possessing its passport, being refugee or resident in Croatia, needed protection from the Fourth Geneva Convention. None of them was treated by Croatian authorities as an enemy citizen. None was repatriated by force to Bosnia-Herzegovina, nor was interned or placed an assigned residence in Croatia. On the contrary, all of them were treated as nationals of the co-belligerent state, enjoying protection of their embassy in Zagreb. So far as I know, the same was true for Croatian citizens in parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina under the control of its central authorities. We can say only besieged Sarajevo. Croatian citizens in besieged Sarajevo were protected by their embassy in Sarajevo. Point (D), finally, the outbreak of hostilities has important effects on intercourse, especially trading between belligerents. In this respect, not conclusive are provisions from treaties of peace concluded in 1919 and 1947 respectively, which settled very much unequal relations on these issues between victorious states and their subjects on the one hand, and vanquished states and their subjects in two world wars on the other. Conclusive is, however, practice of all belligerents during two world wars. From legislation and practices of the United Kingdom, France, the United States in two World Wars, also of Italy and Germany, on trading with enemy, some conclusions may be drawn. Each of belligerents is empowered to prohibit by its laws all trade between its own and enemy subjects, including, of course, their state enterprises. On behalf of these laws in two world wars, practically, all trade and contracting with persons resident in an enemy country or with persons from neutral countries doing business with the enemy, all payments to such persons, and all business and communications with them were interrupted. All contracts made before the entry into force of that legislation were abrogated. Being in contravention with that legislation, all new contracts were null and void and constituted criminal offences. Only contracts concomitant of rights of property, such as leases or mortgages, were not abrogated but they were suspended until the conclusion of peace treaties. Furthermore, all belligerent states seized public enemy property on their owned and on occupied territories, such as funds, ammunition, provisions or rolling stocks of enemy state railways. All these measures were considered by all belligerents as consistent with the law of war which did not suffer changes even after 1945. In relations between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, during all the period up to the conclusion of Dayton Agreement near the end of 1995, it was just opposite what happened, like in respect of diplomatic and treaty relations. Following resolutions of the U.N. Security Council 757, 787 of 1992, and 820 of 1993, commercial, industrial, financial and other intercourse were forbidden in Croatia, and as I know also in Bosnia-Herzegovina only with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and with the Serbian occupied territories in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, but it was the duty of all Member States of the United Nations, including Canada, or the United States or France or others. I have know data, and I cannot give testimony on these matters here, but I'm informed by Defence counsel that they have documents that even shipment of arms and ammunition in contravention to the arms embargo imposed by the Security Council Resolution 713 of 1991 passed through Croatia to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Equally, most of provisions in food, clothing and medicine, which were not transported by air, went to Sarajevo and to other unoccupied parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina through Croatian territory. It would probably be a unique case in history of wars that a belligerent in an international armed conflict helped his enemy by arms and ammunition in such a quantity as Croatia has done for Bosnia-Herzegovina. In addition to the state-to-state relations as I understand it, in the critical period between January 1993 and January 1994, in the zone of responsibility of General Blaskic, no units of Croatian army could penetrate because that area was entirely surrounded by the Bosnia army. Therefore, in that region and in that period, at least there was no international armed conflict, on this account, also, he cannot be indicted for grave breaches of the 1949 Geneva Conventions. It is reported that some units of the Croatian army happened to be outside the Lasva Valley in other areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They mostly consisted of soldiers originating from Bosnia-Herzegovina as I am here, and their presence -- their temporary presence was, in my view, nothing similar to a protracted armed intervention by a foreign state. Lastly, there is no proof that in their zones of operation they exercised competences of an occupying power. From all the above, I came to the following conclusion, I'll read it carefully: State-to-state relations strongly indicate that a state of war or an objective situation of an international armed conflict did not occur between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1993 or afterwards. On the contrary; there is plenty of evidence that two states were co-belligerents in the conflict against Serbian forces, and that the conflict between HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was an unfortunate internal armed conflict. Thank you Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I think after this testimony you would perhaps like to ask some questions, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have any further questions at this time. I would offer Defence Exhibit 468, his curriculum vitae, into evidence, and I also want to assure the professor that although in perhaps diplomatic or academic circles if a party interrupts another it could be a misstep, but please be assured that in the courtroom, when one party makes an objection they're simply following their duty and obligation to their client. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Judges can only agree with what has just been said, that this is part of normal judicial proceedings. Do you have a lot of questions to ask, Mr. Harmon? Would you like to us take a break now? What would you prefer?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would prefer a break now, Mr. President, if that is possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We're going to take a 20 minute break, and we'll resume for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can resume the hearing now, have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, you will allow me, with all the respect that I owe to you, to focus your cross-examination on the direct examination. Don't speak about legal issues, yourself. Don't make law, also.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much, Mr. President and Judge Shahabuddeen. Good morning, Counsel. Cross-examined by Mr. Harmon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor Degan. I'm sorry I interrupted you, but as Counsel has indicated, there are times when a lawyer in court must fulfil his duty. I meant no offence when I interrupted you. Now, let me ask you some questions briefly, and I won't spend too much time, but let me ask you some questions about your testimony. Specifically, you testified that a factor that led you to the conclusion that there was no international armed conflict in Central Bosnia in 1991, 1992 and 1993 was the fact that there was an absence of a declaration, a formal declaration of war. Did I understand your testimony correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the critical period is between January, 1993 and 1994. I think I explained with a lot of arguments of law and facts that there was not an international armed conflict in state-to-state relations between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina as sovereign states and as members of the United Nations, and specifically that in the region of Lasva Valley there was not an international armed conflict, because there were no troops of the Croatian army present there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Degan, you didn't understand my question. I understand your testimony to be that a factor that these Judges should consider in determining whether there was an international armed conflict was the fact that there was no declaration of war between Bosnia and Herzegovina in the Republic of Croatia; did I understand your testimony correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but it was one of the elements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you about that element, we will come to the other elements. Please. And you cited as examples where there was no formal declaration of war, but, in fact, war existed. The situation between Japan and China in 1938. Did I understand that testimony correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, then, Professor Degan, was there an international armed conflict between the FRY and the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I studied that problem carefully --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please put your microphone on. There you go, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I studied the problem carefully of relationship between Croatia and Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on the basis of all elements which I exposed here. But it's my conclusion, I came to the conclusion that there was not an international armed conflict between Croatia and Federal Republic of Yugoslavia because of many elements which I can explain here. Probably it's not important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, did Croatia ever declare war on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I take it your testimony is the absence of a declaration, formal declaration of war between two sovereign states is not dispositive of whether there in fact exists an international armed conflict, it is only one factor to be considered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, I had not opportunity to expose all those elements from the Common Article 2 from four Geneva Conventions in 1949. I wanted to explain that in order to prevent the further discussion, but I am ready to do that now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Professor Degan, while there may have been an absence of a formal declaration of war, was there a recognition, as far as you know, of hostilities that existed, armed hostilities that existed between the Republic of Croatia and the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina during the relevant time period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between governments of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, was there a recognition of the existence of armed hostilities during that time period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I know in the state-to-state relations, there was not such a recognition.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me show you, then, if I could, if I could have the assistance of the usher, I would like to show you some documents, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 556A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Professor Degan, if you could just look at that for a couple of moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you want a little bit of time, Professor? This is the Presiding Judge speaking to you. Professor, do you need some time to read it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Degan, this is a statement of the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it is a result of a session that was held on the 13th of May, 1993 in which it considered the situation in the region of Mostar and Central Bosnia, and in this respect there are certain government conclusions. I would like to direct your attention to, on the English version, the second page, the last paragraph on the second page that reads, "The government of Bosnia and Herzegovina states, once again, that it wishes to develop all encompassing relations in cooperation with the Republic of Croatia on the basis of mutual trust and respect; however, unless the attacks are immediately stopped and the units of the state of Croatia are withdrawn immediately from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina will be forced to turn to the international community and request protection from the aggression." So my question to you is: First of all, were you aware, Professor Degan, at any time during the time frame of 1993 that the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina complained about armed aggression in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina by soldiers from Croatia? Did you ever hear of any such complaints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Chairman, I wanted to explain in my larger text that there can be some differences between the act of aggression and international armed conflict. I mentioned in my intervention this morning that single interventions by the United States in Libya, and this year in Afghanistan and Sudan. Did not generate into any international armed conflict. Such acts which are, which can be acts of aggression can generate into international armed conflicts; and if it happens, then all provisions from Geneva Conventions apply, and then both sides, even the victim of aggression can commit international crimes. But that, what you quoted here, Mr. Prosecutor, it may be the proof of an unlawful intervention by Croatia, internal armed conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina which was not authorised by the U.N. Security Council. But many unlawful armed interventions do not generate into international armed conflicts. I am still of a view that there was an internal armed conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina between HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and perhaps you have some evidence that in some periods temporarily there were some fractions of the Croatian army present in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but that's very far from an international armed conflict. Even the passage you quoted finishes that the "government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina will be forced to turn to the international community and request protection from the aggression." It's not said "international armed conflict." Your document is dated, I don't see a date, it's dated -- maybe you know the date of the document. 13th of May 1993. The declarations and letters of the permanent representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the United Nations are also acts of state. And I can quote you a letter dated on 21st of April, 1993 from the permanent representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the United Nations, to the president of the Security Council, of 21st of April, 1993. I will quote you some parts of this letter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, we may come to that letter in a few minutes if you could refrain for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right, you are in privileged position here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As professors often times --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like things to be clear here. The people who have a privileged position is the Judges. This is the second time that you consider one of the parties has a privileged position. Let me remind you this is a specific procedure, that is one of the International Criminal Tribunal, which has its own procedures, different from others. We are the guardians of equitable proceedings, Professor. I did not interrupt you, but I do not accept you saying that the Prosecutor has a privileged position, only the Judges do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, but if you allow, I would like to cite sections of that letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, go ahead, cite them if you want to, but please don't forget that you must answer the Prosecutor's questions. It is not to give him a privilege. He is asking questions and you have to answer. And, of course, you will answer taking as much time as you consider necessary for the details you want to provide in your answer. Proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. "The recent reports of the conflict between the Bosnia and Herzegovina army and the Croatian Defence Council have been greatly exaggerated as an ethnic conflict between Muslim and Croats. This fighting is not a conflict based along ethnic lines; rather, it is a conflict which is a consequence of the international communities arms embargo on Bosnia and Herzegovina and the International Community's failure to provide adequate humanitarian assistance to the besieged population in Central Bosnia and Herzegovina. This arms embargo denies both Muslims and Croats adequate defence capabilities in the face of barbarous aggression from Serbia and Montenegro. The arms embargo and the lack of adequate sustenance pits neighbour against neighbour for control of scarce resources. If the two armies had adequate defence capabilities, and if the population in Central Bosnia were adequately assisted with humanitarian needs, conflict between local leaders would have never occurred." Thank you, Your Honour. I think it's my answer to the question of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me show you another document, if I could. And this document, Professor Degan, is dated September the 4th, 1993, and you will have a copy of it in front of you in just a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document 557.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document, Professor Degan, is dated September 4, 1993 from a member of the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it is it addressed to UNPROFOR BH command, and UNPROFOR headquarters for the former Yugoslavia. And if you will take just a moment to read it. Professor Degan, this document, again, in light of my previous questions, was there a recognition of the existence of hostilities between the two countries? This is a letter that is from the individual who was a member of the Bosnian presidency, and he describes, does he not in there, attacks by, in Bosnia and Herzegovina by members of the Croatian army and HVO forces? I direct your attention to the second full paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I comment?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, here is also mentioned only the term "Aggression" not "international armed conflict". It dates 4th of September, 1993. Mr. President, with your permission, I can quote another document issued not by one of the parties in that internal armed conflict, but by co-chairman Stoltenberg of 10th of January, 1994 on talks between presidents Izetbegovicvic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Professor. I have a procedural question. Mr. Hayman, your witness is citing documents which the judges don't have. Do you intend to present them? Because there is something inequitable here. The witness is answering through documents, that is his right, but he is the one who knows what is in the documents, he knows his own text, whereas we do not know anything. I would like to know how the Defence considers this call for documents which seem to be very interesting, to be of great interest to the Defence or the accused, but we don't have them. What is your opinion on that, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness has referenced a great many documents in his testimony we have not produced. The fact is it is very time consuming and it greatly lengthens the proceeding to inundate the Tribunal with documents. The tack that the Prosecutor is taking currently is asking the witness "Aren't these documents that tend to indicate armed conflict between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina," which is an empirical question, what do documents reflect, and the witness quite appropriately is responding with similar empirical material concerning what other documents contain. I haven't seen the document he is referencing. This is, I think, the nature of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am going to object at some point in time, Mr. President, I ask the witness a question, he doesn't answer my question but he refers to other documents. I would like him to focus on the question that I asked him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What I would like is for you to focus on the answer. If you need to refer to documents you can do so, but refer to them -- only first of all give us your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My answer is that in the document the Prosecution presented to this Trial Chamber mentions inter alia, "to put an end to the aggression against our country as soon as possible." It was alleged that in some parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina with Muslim population, they were attacked by over 5.000 members of the Croatian army and HVO forces. This is a document by one side in an internal armed conflict. Even by those data, if they were accurate, nobody can prove that there was an international armed conflict between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, if those data were accurate, then it would be again an unlawful armed intervention by the units of Croatian army in Bosnia-Herzegovina. For instance, the United States intervened in many other countries and probably most of those armed interventions were acts of aggression, but they did not bring it to international armed conflicts. Thank you. That's my answer, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Degan, in addition to these examples wherein the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was indicating that there were hostilities between forces of the Republic of Croatia and their own forces, there were United Nations resolutions demanding the withdrawal of Croatian troops from Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I specifically refer to resolution 752 dated the 15th of May, 1992 and U.N. Security Council 787, also making a similar demand. Have you seen those resolutions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know those resolutions, but they relate to the time which precedes the critical period for which General Blaskic was accused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you agree, do you not, you don't dispute that the United Nations in two resolutions demanded that Croatian army forces be withdrawn from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I agree, there is resolution 787 of 16th of November, 1992, but perhaps it relates to the crime of General Blaskic, but I am not sure in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you, if I could, a document which is found, it's Prosecutor's Exhibit 406/95.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If you don't have enough copies for everybody, put it on the ELMO so that the Judges can see it, because we don't have the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This, Professor Degan, is a letter dated the 28th of January, 1994, from the permanent representative of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the United Nations, addressed to the president of the Security Council. You will see attached to the second page an annex, and you will see on the annex there is a description of the military intervention of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia against the sovereign and independent Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And you will see in reviewing that particular document dated the 28th of January, 1994, a description of the units from the Republic of Croatia that were in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And you will see, sir, the last paragraph, and I will quote the last paragraph, "We express our deepest concern about such an extent of military intervention of the Republic of Croatia in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and request that Security Council to firmly condemn such activities and take all necessary measures in accordance with the provisions of Chapter 7 of the United Nations charter and all the relevant general assembly and Security Council resolutions." So, Professor Degan, you have cited some examples of, in Libya, an example of an intervention in Libya, which consisted of, as I recall, a single bombing incident. You have cited an example of Afghanistan attacked by the United States on alleged terrorist camps in Afghanistan which consisted of a single bombing attack. And you have now seen three documents I have shown you, the earliest document is May 13th, 1993, these are examples, and the latest document is a letter dated the 28th of January, 1994, and you have seen two Security Council resolutions, those being resolution 752 and 787 dealing with Croatian troops present in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And my question to you, Professor Degan, is: Was there a recognition both by the states themselves, by Bosnia and by the United Nations, that hostilities between two sovereign states was, in fact, occurring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor, that was a letter of one side. Perhaps there were present some troops of Croatian army, but I tried to prove before this Tribunal that an element of an international armed conflict should be its protracted character in time and intensity. With your permission, Mr. President, I would now quote Mr. Thorvald Stoltenberg's report, which dates almost at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could have a copy of that report before Professor Degan quotes it, then I might be able to ask questions of Professor Degan in respect of that particular report. I find myself disadvantaged.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I add a comment, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, you may, but let me remind you though the Judges don't have this report. We would like to have it. Perhaps we should suspend so we could have it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, General Blaskic was accused for grave breaches of Geneva Conventions in that very closed area of his responsibility, which was besieged by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There was no presence of troops of the Croatian army, that region of responsibility of General Blaskic. To accuse General Blaskic for consequences of the presence of Croatian troops in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina would be tantamount to accusing him for the crime of aggression, and Mr. Blaskic was of so low of a commanding position that he cannot be guilty of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Professor, let me remind you, I don't want to have to do it again, you're not here as the Defence counsel for the accused. He has his counsel, and they will argue in respect of the documents that have been provided here. You are a Defence witness. Let me remind you to remain within the scope of your testimony for the Defence. However, if you rely significantly on this report, the Prosecution doesn't have it, and apparently the Defence doesn't have it either, neither do the Judges, and we would like to have the report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, that's not it. If you're going to base yourself on the report, could you give it to the Defence, the Prosecution, unless you decide not to use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Maybe it can be put on the ELMO and he can read from it, Mr. President. That way everyone can see what he's reading from and we can proceed. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would still like a copy of any report that Professor Degan reads from, so I can look at the rest of the report, those portions he has not read from.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just want to note that there have been lots of occasions in this trial where the Prosecutor or indeed I have asked a question and quoted a document or a source. It does not automatically follow, therefore, that we have to suspend the hearing, make copies and circulate it for everyone. I have no problem providing this document. I haven't see it, I don't know exactly what it is, the Professor has far-ranging factual knowledge, but I suggest we can put it on the ELMO and we can read from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We're going to put the document on the ELMO, but it must be provided to the Prosecution, and it will appear in the Judges' case file under a number that the registrar will give us. For the time being we can continue the proceedings. I would ask the Professor, who speaks French very well, perhaps he could put his headset on, because apparently I'm not sure he heard what I have to say, and I really want you to hear what I have to say. That's my privilege, my little privilege. Therefore, please put the headset on. You speak French very well, but sometimes you don't quite hear what I'm saying. So if you don't mind, please put on the headset and I think that will facilitate everybody's work. For the time being we will resume the proceedings, and then the report will be provided to the Prosecution and will appear in the Judges' case file. All right. We want to hear what you have to say, Professor. I'm sure that you understand me even better now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. No, in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the report by Thorvald Stoltenberg of 10th of January, 1994 on talks in Bonn between President Itzebegovic and Tudjman. I'll quote paragraphs 3 and 4. Paragraph 4 is more important. In paragraph 3 it's written: "President Tudjman, in his draft treaty on future relations between Croat and Muslims, advanced the idea of a confederation between the Republic of Croatia and the Muslims and Croat parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Nevertheless, he would like to see the boundaries defined between the areas allocated to the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims. President Itzebegovic, on the other hand, is not in favour of such a delimitation but would like to achieve agreement that the two components should have around 51 per cent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Each side maintained its position on that issue." The paragraph 4 is more important, because it directly relates to the responsibility of General Blaskic: "On Central Bosnia, President Itzebegovic would clearly like to have Croat pockets such as Vitez, Busovaca, Kiseljak, Kresevo, Vares, Novi Travnik, Fojnica and Gornji Vakuf included in the Muslim majority area. President Tudjman, for his part, is not prepared to concede this. Part of the problem has to do with a munitions factory at Vitez and three munition factories at Novi Travnik that each side would like to have. President Itzebegovic openly expressed his determination to fight for the plant at Vitez, while President Tudjman was equally firm that he could not have it. Both sides are aware that current BiH offences against Vitez have this objective in mind." I find -- there is, I think, another -- yeah. In point seven, second page. That's the conclusion: "The Muslims having scored victories in Central Bosnia and knowing that the Serbs are under the burden of sanctions, are demonstrating confidence in their ability to win more territories through military action. Indications from various capitals that all parties must co-operate in the search for a negotiated settlement have come at the same time as calls have been voiced in the NATO summit for more vigorous military action ." So those quotations go in favour of innocence of General Blaskic, but I'll not comment anymore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Professor Degan, during the war in 1993 in Bosnia, did you ever travel to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately I did not, but if you are interested in my personal situation, my mother lived in Sarajevo, and she died in January 1995 when the city was still besieged. I could not penetrate to the city for the funeral of my mother. She was victim of aggression from surrounding mountains of the Serbian part. I have some other very sorry experience of my sister's destiny. Her only son perished in the battle of Herzegovina, but it's better that I do not explain. I can only say I was for the first time in Sarajevo two years ago. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, do you know the extent to which Croatia had its troops in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only from documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the geographic extent of their penetration into Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina I know better than others, and I know especially well the valley of Lasva where I passed my vacations -- summer vacations in 1946, '47, before General Blaskic was born. I know also the valley of Neretva. I passed it many times by car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you testify today about your opinions, you are -- don't know the facts about how many Croatian army troops were deployed in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, how far those troops penetrated northward into Bosnia and Herzegovina; do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only legally qualify the presence of troops of Croatian army in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and my conclusion is that it was not a protracted armed conflict between two states, it was unlawful armed intervention without authorisation of the U.N. Security Council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you, you also testified about various agreements that existed between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and you cited an agreement on friendship and co-operation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that a treaty or was that an agreement, and is there a difference in International Law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I understood, it was a treaty governed by the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties. There is not such a difference from the point of view of Public International Law, between agreements and treaties. There is some difference in the American practice but not in International Law practice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen a copy of that Agreement on Friendship and Co-operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you tell the Court what other treaties existed between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- Mr. President, I quoted all of that which I collected from the Croatian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and I can quote them again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, tell me what they are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I read a few.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just tell me what they are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a moment. Both countries were victims of aggression from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Both countries got their independence in that very unhappy time for both of them, and because the treaties of the predecessor state do not regulate the bilateral relations between successor states, a new set of treaties must be concluded between all successor states. In this respect, I find -- I'll find. Just a moment. There were very few treaties before January 1993. Just a moment. I mentioned the agreement between governments -- I mentioned the agreement between governments of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia before the international recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina and before of proclamation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so one can suspect, in the real nature of that agreement, it's of -- it's of -- I think in -- on refugees in Croatia. I mentioned that treaty -- excuse me. I cannot find here everything I wanted. There was an agreement of 14th of April that the diplomatic and consular missions of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina abroad will protect interests of nationals of the other state party where only one of them had such a mission. I know personally that that agreement was applied, because at that very time I was -- I happened to be in Brussels at the conference on former Yugoslavia. The representatives of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia in that city were in close co-operation. Then came the Agreement of Friendship and Co-operation of 21st July, 1992. After it, 25th of July agreement on establishment of diplomatic relations between two states. As I know, until January 1993 there were no other bilateral treaties, but for the -- for the existence of the international armed conflict, important is the faith of those bilateral treaties in a situation of an armed conflict like that which happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina. No party cancelled any of those agreements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your testimony, in response to my question, was there were very few such agreements, perhaps two or three at the most?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably four or five.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Four or five. All right. Now, let me ask you: You said that at the outbreak of hostilities, certainly normal diplomatic relations is a measure of whether or not there is or is not international armed conflict. Were you aware, Professor Degan, that after the embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina was established in Zagreb, that the funds supporting that mission in Zagreb were seized?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know. I don't know for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is the seizure of funds of a diplomatic mission in Croatia normal? Is that an indication that diplomatic relations between the two sovereign states is conducted in a normal fashion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If it really happened, then it would be in breach of the 1961 Vienna Convention of diplomatic -- of diplomatic relations. I don't know for that what you allege here, but even if such an unlawful act was committed, it did not bring to the rupture of diplomatic relations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you testified as well that the citizens who -- from Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Muslims who found refuge in the Republic of Croatia, you said that no citizen was forcibly repatriated; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not forcefully repatriated to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that was the practice of belligerents in two world wars or even in French Prussian war of 1870, '71. Most of them wanted to go to third states, that's true, but that's not a measure of a belligerent state if it allows them to go, for instance, to Germany or to Switzerland.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can it force them to go to a third state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That you allege, not me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not alleging anything, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you if a state can forcibly send citizens who seek refuge into in this case the Republic of Croatia, can send those citizens to a third state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Croatia, in that very time, do you think it was -- it happened in 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1993. Still the situation with a mass of displaced persons and refugees in Croatia was difficult. Croatia got some help for refugees and those persons, but there were too many, that perhaps something happened what you said here, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not -- it was not an act of a belligerent state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that Croatia did not repatriate back to Bosnia any Muslim refugees in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I know, it did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you, you testified that Croatia also supplied arms to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Bosnia and Herzegovina, and you indicated that that was an indication of normal state relations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware, Professor, that when the Bosnian -- Croat Bosnian Muslim war broke out that the Republic of Croatia stopped sending arms to the Bosnian Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Defence counsel told me they had two testimonies which will follow me who will talk about that problem. Certainly I am not a person to testify to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you some documents as my next exhibit, and while these are being prepared perhaps, Mr. President, we could go into private session with these particular documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. It's almost five to one. Do you have a lot of questions? I suppose quite a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On these documents, Mr. President, it will just take a few minutes, but I think it's best we proceed in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, we'll move into private session. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Resume the hearing now. Registrar, have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And have the witness brought in as well, please, Professor Degan. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Professor, have you rested up a bit? Is everything all right? All right, we will continue with the cross-examination. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, good afternoon Mr. President, Judge Shahabuddeen, Counsel, and good afternoon Professor Degan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your testimony you stated that, and I'm quoting you from the transcript on your point A, "The outbreak of war has as its immediate effect rupture of diplomatic and consular relations between belligerent states. Nothing similar happened between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia. Embassies of the two states of Zagreb and Sarajevo respectively exercised unimpeded all of their functions since the establishment of diplomatic relations near the end of 1992." If I could have the assistance of the usher, I would like to pass out the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document 559.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Degan, this document consists of two documents appended together. The first is a communication from the ambassador of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Croatia to the president of the presidency, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. And she indicates in her letter, "Please find attached information of the freezing of the account of the embassy which in effect renders the operation of the embassy impossible." And this is dated January the 7th, 1994. Now, the second part of this document, please take some time to read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you have a text in English? It's more useful to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a translation that is unofficial, so --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right, then I will look at the original.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you have relevant parts that you want to have read out? Because the Judges would like to have the translation once the witness has looked at the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Perhaps we could put it on the ELMO and the interpreters could read the second -- is it possible that the interpretation booth could read this document in French and in English?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The entire document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If you allow for the transcript it would be better that somebody in the courtroom were to read the document and then if possible we could ask the witness to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will ask the witness to assist us in reading the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Or Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor, if you would read the document, both documents, then, starting with --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have two pieces, but I think that's one document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you read the first page of the document, the short letter?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this is not the document we have on the ELMO. This is not the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I need to put another document on the ELMO, first, the first page. We are now in a position if you would kindly assist us in reading the document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Let me also remind the witness that he should read slowly, a bit more slowly than he was doing, for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That document was addressed to the president of presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Izetbegovic, to the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to the Minister of Foreign Affairs who was at the time Mr. Ivan Ljubjankic. Now I proceed reading each in original Croat or Bosnian language. "Please find attached information concerning the freezing of the account of the embassy which practically makes it impossible for the embassy to operate." The document is dated 7th of January, 1994. "Embassy of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Zagreb. Reference: Explanation of the impossibility of allocating resources from the nonresidential account of the embassy of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Zagreb because the resources were blocked on the 6th of January, 1994. "On the 6th of January, 1994, the embassy of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was informed by Zagrebicka Banka, a bank, address Savska number 60, foreign services department. The council of legal officers of the mentioned bank passed a decision to block the resources on the nonresidential account of the embassy of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina up to 260.202 Deutschemark, German marks. The decision was passed on the basis of the ruling of the district economic court in Zagreb, number R1, 162/93, on the basis of reference number 393387/93. Proceedings related to this have not been completed yet. From a economic point of view the embassy of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Zagreb is not in a position to use its own resources on this account or the resources from possible inflows which makes it totally impossible to operate on the territory of the Republic of Croatia. Also the fact should be highlighted that foreign exchange payments in cash are in contravention of the legal provisions of the Republic of Croatia from this field and the cash payments in the currency of the Republic of Croatia, the Croatian dinar, makes it impossible for the embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina to use tax facilities as a diplomatic representation and tax alleviation to which it is entitled. Otherwise, all enterprises have to take a certain amount of cash payments by way of a tax up to a certain percentage depending on the goods being purchased. In addition to that, even in the case of cash payments without tax facilities or tax exemptions it is very difficult to provide for the conversion of larger sums of foreign currencies into the currency of the Republic of Croatia in official exchange offices. The accounting department of the embassy of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." INTERPRETER: The date is not on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your assistance, Professor Degan. Let me ask you some questions about this document now and then I will permit you to make some comments on the document.
