But first of all, this document shows there was apparently a domestic court decision that attached some kind of a lien against the assets of the Bosnian embassy. Do you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document proves that a bank blocked the funds, and it's obviously in violation of the 1961 Vienna Convention on diplomatic relations. It is not the act of state. And that is what I could also comment, is that it happened on 7th of January, 1994. That's just before the time of the Washington agreement with which the armed conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina was stopped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, are you aware that this, that in spite of repeated requests by the Bosnian embassy to the Croatian embassy that those funds remained frozen for at least eight months?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't see it from this text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm giving you information and asking you, in respect of the information that I have provided you, while this does not appear to be an act of state, should the state immediately regulate a problem of this nature involving an embassy of a separate sovereign state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The state was obliged to prevent such acts, but -- can I add? I don't see the personal responsibility of Mr. Blaskic in the Lasva Valley for such an unlawful act.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can assure you he didn't seize these funds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's not the question that was asked of you, Professor. You're very adroit, but that is not quite the question he asked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me change the subject to a different direction and ask you, Professor Degan, if in 1993, was there, in fact, a war going on in the Lasva Valley between forces of the Bosnian government and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was an internal armed conflict between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Croatia allied with the HVO in that conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was unhappily involved in such an internal armed conflict, it was involved on both sides but mostly on the part of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your testimony is that, as far as you know, in the conflict between the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats, the Republic of Croatia supported the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was told that at that time there was some help at least for passage of arms of ammunition through Croatian territory to the other side in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, though, aside from what you were told, whether the Republic of Croatia, which side of the conflict the Republic of Croatia supported in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in between, but it was mostly friendly to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you, then, do you know who General Bobetko is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Bobetko is a Croatian General who was appointed as the commander of the southern front --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Commanding Croatian units in the southern front; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me show you Exhibit 406/10. Mr. Dubuisson, while this is being shown on the ELMO, if you could get 406/16 and 406/20, it would expedite the matter. Professor, you have in front of you Prosecutor's Exhibit 406/10, and this is an order dated the 20th of April, 1992 by General Bobetko, and in it you will see and can see that General Bobetko appoints officers of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would very much appreciate your views on this particular document, given that this is a Croatian General appointing Bosnian Croats to positions within a military of a separate sovereign state. What is your view on this, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My view is that it happened in time of joint operations of HVO and army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatian army against Serbian forces. It was dated 20th of April, 1992. And on this list I don't see the name of Mr. Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, now if I could show you 406/16 and 406/20. Professor, we will start with 406/16, it is a document dated the 19th of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the critical period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And let me ask you, Professor, this is a document that establishes a command in Central Bosnia, in Gornji Vakuf, and it appoints Brigadier Zarko Tole as commander of that particular command. The second document, Professor, is dated the 14th of June, 1992, and it is also from General Bobetko, and it is, if you turn to paragraph 3.1 on that document, it is an order for offensive operations in which General Bobetko orders forces of the HVO to move in certain directions and take certain actions in a military campaign. What is your reaction to these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My reaction is the same. It happened before the critical period for which the General Blaskic was accused, and that was the period of alliance of army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, HVO and Croatian army in the battle against the Serbian enemy. That's my comment, and I forgot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, did Croatian soldiers fight against Bosnian army forces in Bosnia in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw some documents which prove the presence of some units of the Croatian army, not in the Lasva Valley, but in some other parts of Herzegovina, and the border region between Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is not just the presence of Croatian soldiers in Bosnia, my question to you was: Did Croatian soldiers engage in armed conflict --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Against the forces of the legitimate government of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from those documents, it proceeds they were engaged in the battle. But it's the tricky question whether before that unhappy armed conflict both armies recognised themselves, and is the question whether even the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina recognised the HVO, and vice versa. But I must agree that the presence of some units of Croatian army, although they were probably mostly originating from Bosnia-Herzegovina, as I was, and although they were not very distinguishable from the HVO, was an unlawful armed intervention in that unhappy internal armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time I need to show the witness certain documents under seal, and if we could go into private session I would like to show him certain documents and ask for his comments. Mr. Dubuisson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We'll move for -- into a private session for a few moments. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, you were asked about the conflict between Japan and China in 1938 and whether there was a formal declaration of war in 1938. In that conflict were the other factors you've identified for an international armed conflict, other than a formal declaration of war, were they present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was an ongoing armed conflict which in fact started in 1928 with the Japanese bombing of the city of Shanghai, and later on there was invasion and occupation of Manchuria and creation of a puppet state of Pandrakua, and if I remember well, in 1937 there was a full-fledged offensive by Japanese army to the northern part of China, and they came to the bridge of Peking. They stopped, and then it was recognised by both states that war existed. In that specific conflict both parties had interests for the time being not to recognise the state of war. The Chinese government, both the quantities of arms from the United States, if they recognised the state of war because of the isolationist policy of the United States of that time, it would be stopped. On the other side, Japan did not want to recognise the war for not being aggressor in that war. So it was an unusual situation, and I can prove that the international armed conflict between Japan and China started at least 1937.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have a document if I could have assistance to hand out, this is the letter of 21 April, 1993 that the Professor referred to earlier in his testimony, and I wanted to put that into the record and have him identify it as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can we have the number for the Stoltenberg report that was requested by the Trial Chamber? What is the Defence number for that?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For that document, the Stoltenberg report, it is D469; and this one is 470.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, I would like to ask you, is this the letter that you were referring to earlier in your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you agree in paragraph 4 of this letter that the permanent representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the United Nations at the time referred to the conflict in Central Bosnia as a conflict between local leaders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I quoted it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked about examples of military intervention, including unlawful military intervention, as opposed to a state of international armed conflict, and the two examples mentioned by the Prosecutor were the American bombings of Libya and Afghanistan. Can you give the Court any other examples of military interventions, including unlawful military intervention, as distinguished from a state of international armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. For instance, the Soviet intervention in Prague, Czechoslovakia in 1968, it generated into an occupation of the country which did not last for a long time because there were some new agreements with the puppet Czechoslovak regime, and there were also armed interventions by the United States, in the Dominican Republic, 1965, that was an intervention of I think six member states of the organisation of American states, including the U.S. Army. There was an intervention in Grenada by the United States which lasted at least for some weeks in the period of the Reagan Administration. That which was the bloodiest was probably the American armed intervention of Panama. If I remember well, it happened 1980. It lasted for some time. The Panama City was bombed and there were many civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for those additional examples. You were asked about provision of military assistance, and to what extent the existence of such aid or the absence of such aid may indicate the presence or absence of an international armed conflict. May it also be an indicia of the presence or absence of an international armed conflict if a state sells munitions to another state or if that state allows the transhipment of munitions through its territory to the other state? Could you comment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be proof to the opposite.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Namely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For instance, the United States massively helped Israel, by arms and credits, and Israel committed some acts of unlawful intervention against third states, mostly in Lebanon, but there were not acts of the United States government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you about the reverse, that is, if, for example, Croatia, in 1993, did not donate arms to the BH army, but if they allowed the transhipment of arms through the Croatian territory to the BH army and sold arms to the BH army, is that an indicia in any way of the presence or absence of an international armed conflict between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a proof of the absence of the armed conflict between those two sovereign states.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Hayman. Let me now turn to my colleague, Judge Shahabuddeen. Now you're going to answer questions that the Judge wishes to ask you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Professor Degan, I would like personally to welcome you and to thank you for the help which you have come to give the Court in unravelling and understanding many of the complicated issues in a relatively mysterious area of law. Thank you. Now, would I be right, sir, in understanding your presentation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: In understanding your presentation -- perhaps you would like to put on the earphone, because I'm a chronically soft speaker. I ought to apologise to you. Would I be right in understanding your presentation to be based essentially on the distinction between an international armed conflict and an armed intervention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, armed intervention is an unlawful act if it's not authorised by the Security Council or if it doesn't happen in self-defence. I tried to explain here that some sorts of armed intervention can generate into international armed conflicts, but not all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I give you time to think it out, not that you need to think it out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But we should also discuss the different levels of intervention in International Law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, Professor, would I also be right in thinking that your application of that distinction to the facts of this case, as you understand the facts, means this: Yes, Croatia had armed forces within Bosnia-Herzegovina, but that amounted not to an international armed conflict but only to armed intervention; is that your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my position was that it was probably an unlawful armed intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then would I also be right, sir, in understanding you to mean that in determining whether there was an international armed conflict, two criteria were applicable. One, the duration in time of the relationship of hostility; and two, the intensity of the hostility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I tried to explain that there are many elements, some elements of existence of international armed conflicts are provided in Article 2 of the 1949 Geneva Conventions, and one in Article -- first of the protocol of 1977, and I added some other criteria, so the sum, or all those criteria applied on the actual situation could lead to a conclusion whether an international armed conflict existed or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I accept that. May I rephrase it this way: That your presentation suggested that two of the most applicable criteria in the circumstances of this case were, one, the duration in time of the hostilities, and two, the intensity of the hostilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are among other criteria. I tried to prove on the basis of some other criteria from the wartime practice that it was not an international armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: In other words, I would understand your position, I'm sure everybody would think it most reasonable, that the final conclusion would depend on the facts of each case; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but there is another tricky problem before the criminal jurisdiction like this one, the personal guilt of an accused person; but that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Sometimes the problem is apt to be complicated by this reflection which experience will be that ever so often words used by one party or another do not exactly match the facts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It sometimes happens, but I think not so much in relations between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, because there were some declarations from which it could be concluded that an international armed conflict didn't exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You would say that is a complicating factor in the analysis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Happily for us lawyers, our profession would not exist if all facts are simple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Exactly so, exactly so. Now, I have a problem on the bench in that unfortunately I didn't take a note of the exhibit number of a certain document. So I will hold it up and hope that our registrar and counsel will be able to come to my help. It's a statement of the government of the -- 556A, I wonder if the registrar would be so kind as to put it before you. Now, would you very kindly turn to page 2, paragraph 3. This is a statement made on 13th of May, 1993. Now, in paragraph 3 you see references being made by Bosnia-Herzegovina to partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina, its confederalisation and so forth. In other words, Bosnia-Herzegovina is accusing Croatia of making statements of this kind. You see that part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, I'm not asking you whether you agree or not that such statements were made. I am only asking you about your reaction to the distinction suggested between partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina and its confederalisation. Do you see a distinction there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not say that such declarations of which I am aware proves the objective situation of international armed conflict, but I agree with you that that was an unhappy policy from the Croatian side which did not help the mutual trust between not only Croats and Bosnians in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but also with the decent Serbian population of that country. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me pick your fertile brain a little further. Would I be right, Professor, in understanding this reference to partition on the one hand and confederalisation on the other to mean this: That in the case of confederalisation the component units of Bosnia-Herzegovina would remain within the same state, but that in the case of partition, this would not be so, the state would split into two different states on the plane of international relations. Is that understanding right or wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I remember well of Croatian official declarations, it was not the word of partition in official declarations but of confederalisation or federalisation, probably. Confederalisation and federation are, from the point of view of International Law, the unity is very much different, because confederation is a union of sovereign states, on the basis of an international treaty, and federation is based on the federal constitution. I can only say that those designs did not help to stop the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So do I understand you to mean this: That even in the case of confederalisation, each of the component units would be a sovereign state on the plane of International Law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And do I then understand you to mean that each of these two concepts, partition or confederalisation, would rupture the previous integrity of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am very lucky that it did not realise this. The situation was settled first by the Washington Agreement in the beginning of 1994, and finally by the Dayton Agreement. So there were some designs with which personally I don't agree, but happily that internal armed conflict was stopped. It did not generate into an international armed conflict. I hope the same will happen in Kosovo, the development can be very much similar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Shall we all observe a little restraint in our references to Kosovo for reasons which would be obvious to you as a distinguished international lawyer. Now, let us talk about partition. Did you ever learn of any allegation of an agreement between the Republic of Croatia and Serbia Montenegro to divide Bosnia-Herzegovina between those two states?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I read a lot in Croatian press about it criticising it, and I read also in the press that my elderly colleague academician Bilandzic was here testifying on those talks, but I have no personal experience about that. I was not present at Karadjordjevo and I was -- unlike him, I was not, as an expert, involved in the Serbian delegation on working on any maps. It was the position I liked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Professor, I don't know who was at Karadjordjevo and who was not, and, of course, I take it from you you were not there, but you had heard that there was an agreement made at Karadjordjevo between the Presidents of Croatia and Serbia Montenegro to divide Bosnia-Herzegovina between those two states. Did you hear of that in the press or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were accusations by Croatian opposition of the policy of the Croatian president in that respect, but I have no data or documents that it happened or that it didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me put it hypothetically this way to you: If the Court should find that there was an agreement between Croatia and Serbia Montenegro to divide Bosnia-Herzegovina between them, then would you say that that would influence your position that the presence of Croatian armed forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina mounted only to an armed intervention and not to an international armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably my view would be that that was a political cause, very serious cause for the conflict, but that still that conflict remained on the level of an internal armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me ask you another question of fact. Did you learn of any allegations to the effect that the Republic of Croatia planned to annex Herceg-Bosna as a component part of the Republic of Croatia after Bosna-Herceg would have succeeded in severing its ties with Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Personally, I don't know on that, but I know even before the aggression of the Yugoslav army against Bosnia-Herzegovina happened some factions of population only in Herzegovina wanted to -- they wanted to join Croatian with their territory, but you know, my personal situation is very much different. My family lived in Sarajevo where Croats are a minority. My mother died there, and I was born in Bosanski Brod, that's a small city on the boarder line with Croatian on the river of Sava and populations from Bosanski Posavina and Sarajevo really did not want to change the boarder lines of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I could say the most of that population. Maybe there were some extremes. I really don't know whether the most of Croats from Herzegovina really wanted to join the Croatian state or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Professor, I didn't know of these personal difficulties which you and your family suffered, and I take the opportunity of letting you know very sincerely how deeply I sympathise with you. I really mean that. Now, tell me this: Would you say the analysis of the situation is slightly complicated by an opposition between two forces? By this I mean, was it the case that the Republic of Croatia had two competing objectives in Bosnia-Herzegovina? On the one hand, the Republic of Croatia would wish to calibrate with the government with the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina in a common cause against Serbia Montenegro. On the other hand, the Republic of Croatia stood opposed to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina insofar as the Republic of Croatia supported the HVO in its struggle against the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Was that the situation, the opposition between two forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, probably the political situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina and relations between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina were even more complicated. There were different views, different ambitions of the future of two states and their relationship. There were some extremist views which were friendly to the partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but on the other hand, probably on the side of the Bosnian army there were extremists, there were fundamentalists who also committed crimes in that unhappy -- unhappy war. As I remember from my experience, my lifetime in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you will find even now some Croats who are more friendly to Serbs than to Muslims. There are some -- and vice versa. There are Muslims who are more friendly to Croats than Serbs and vice versa, and it's the same with Serbs. It's interesting that in some parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina that friendship between all three groups survived even this disastrous war. For instance, the small city of Visoko and some other places. But because of some historic events in some other part, in eastern Herzegovina, there were clashes between Serbian and Muslim sides, in the beginning on the First World War, at the end of that war, in the Second World War and so on. And unfortunately, if I understand well, in those regions of Bosnia-Herzegovina where Croats are in some majority, there was a sentiment more friendly to Serbs than to Muslims. Also, I found many Muslims from Mostar who are not -- who are hostile to Croats from Herzegovina. So the situation is very complicated, and everybody suffers for it. Maybe it's not the answer which satisfies you, but the picture is not black and white.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then -- I appreciate that very much. That is not the least of the problems which the bench has to face. The picture is not black and white. We have to navigate very carefully between facts which are not all easily reconcilable. So I come to my last question on which I would like the benefit of your assistance. I've put to you, my impression is that you accept it in substance, that the Republic of Croatia was pursuing two competing aims in Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the one hand, it would like to have Sarajevo in a common struggle against the Serbs. On the other hand, it was opposed to Sarajevo insofar as it supported the HVO in its struggle against Sarajevo. Now, the question which I put to you is this: Would you say that insofar as the Republic of Croatia offered military assistance to Sarajevo, that assistance was rendered in pursuance of the first aim, and that aim was to help Sarajevo in the common cause which the two governments were prosecuting against the Serbs. It had nothing to do with the help which Croatia was giving to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the Croatian government there were some people from Herzegovina who probably followed the line of the conflict with Bosnia-Herzegovina, and perhaps of its partition. So the situation is so complicated that I would not like to give you my opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then, Professor, it remains for me to say how much I appreciate the guarded terms of your reply, and to wish you well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Professor Degan, I would like to add my thanks to yours for Judge Shahabuddeen's contribution, which characterises his traditional modesty. Of course, things are not always black and white, and frequently we have arguments over the grey areas. I have very few questions for you. For my two or three questions, I would like to go back to the distinction you made when you characterised the situation that we have to judge, that is the distinction between the international armed conflict, legally speaking, which was well constituted, and for which I would like to congratulate you for your competence which you showed. You also indicated the fact that there was a certain duration and a certain intensity. I don't want to go back to what the Prosecutor already asked or those that my own colleague Judge Shahabuddeen asked, but I would like to know within this concept of intensity you include a constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and, therefore, of the HVO. How would you characterise, in respect of the international armed conflict, the assistance and support to the constitution of a kind of confederation which is known as a political administrative entity, that is Bosna-Herceg, or do you put that back into the duration and intensity which are the two major factors in the international armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not very pleased that I did not have the opportunity here to present my entire text which is made up of 40 pages in which the different problems which are the subject of the many questions that the Prosecutor asked are covered. However, I discussed the problems of intensity only in respect of the existence of an international armed conflict. The same criteria should also be present in a domestic conflict within the framework of a single country. And I found that that element was present in armed conflicts between the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, including the Lasva Valley. As regards the establishment of Herceg-Bosna, perhaps in 1990 or 1991 that was an initiative of the local population mostly from eastern Herzegovina, which wanted to join in with the Republic of Croatia, which was in the process of acquiring its full sovereignty and independence. Perhaps it was not so much the ambitions of the Croatian leaders but the desire of the local population, that is the Croatian population, in a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I have already said that in Sarajevo, in Bosanska Posavina, the majority of the Croats wanted to maintain the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know whether my answer has satisfied you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, in part it satisfies me, but I might supplement it by asking you whether a situation like the one we are aware of is unique. Is it unprecedented or could you attach it to precedence in other conflicts that are known as international?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably the most similar one would be the one in Lebanon. That would probably be the most similar conflict because in Lebanon there are actually four religions, and within each religious community there were factions that fought against one another. There were different types of Sunnis, Shiites, Christians. The situation in Lebanon was very complicated, and I was pleased to have a colleague among the members of the members of the Institute for International Law who came from Beruit, and when the conflict in the former Yugoslavia began, I asked him what we should do under the conditions of internal or international armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have only one other question to ask you. You have alluded to -- actually, more than alluded to the intervention -- an intervention of that type would certainly commit the criminal responsibility of the leaders. I'm a criminal Judge, therefore, this was of interest to me; therefore, I would like to know what leaders. And my second question, at what point do you stop the chain of command or the chain of the leaders? Could you make a comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Your Honour, the crimes committed against peace were covered only in the Nuremberg Tribunal statutes and the Tokyo Tribunal statutes. Afterwards, we have a definition for crimes of aggression in the Code that was drafted by the International Law Commission. We know what happened during the conference in Rome. By adopting the Statute for the future International Criminal Court, there was an Article which provided for the jurisdiction of that new court which would be to punish crimes of aggression, but no provisions were made for a definition of aggression. That problem was postponed for the conference which is to take place seven years after the entry into force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Let me stop you there, because I do know that my question -- I'm sure it's my fault and it's my question that led you a bit astray from where I wanted you to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pardon me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I realise you want to finish what you have to say about the International Court but I have another question I wanted to get into. Well, go ahead. Your great knowledge allows me to give you back the floor, but please be brief.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The contracting parties did not want to give jurisdiction to the Court over that crime. In my opinion, the definition of crimes against peace and crimes against -- crimes of aggression show that it is only the political leaders or the military leaders at the highest levels who could be accused should a criminal court be endowed with such jurisdiction, which is the not the case today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. I think that we've got a bit aside from where I wanted to go. I had not properly interpreted something that you were saying. You were saying that it was not an international conflict, in some sort of way it was a legal intervention with this being understood by the Croatian leaders, which continued over a certain amount of time with a certain intensity, but that's not what characterises international crimes. But such initiatives could bring with them criminal responsibility I had thought, and this is my question, that you were getting away from Article 2, but that you were leaving open the entire scope of the Tribunal's statute, which is, of course, not the great International Court that we're all expecting and waiting for, but which do exist in this institution where you've come today. Perhaps I was wrong. Perhaps you were only thinking of crimes of aggression.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was thinking about crimes of aggression. I compared the situation with the Nicaragua case before the court in The Hague, which did not have the jurisdiction to punish the President of the United States. That was my intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can allow the other institutions to think about what you have to say. As far as I'm concerned, I have said all I have to say. You might be surprised to see we're not wearing robes. That is because one of our colleagues is unavailable, which means that with the agreement of the accused and the Defence, we are acting as presiding officers in order to hear your testimony. It is self-evident that has consequences, both legal and judicial, that is, our third colleague, who we are pleased to hear is getting better, when he reads the transcript may have some questions to ask you, may have, and that means that you might have to come back again and then we would have the pleasure of listening once again. I know that's not a convenient thing for you and I'm sorry, but I have nothing further to say to you. I would like to speak for my colleague, who has already said this, and myself, to thank you for coming here. I apologise to the interpreters, but I didn't want to interrupt the testimony. Now we will try to make up for the time we spent by taking a 30-minute not a 20-minute pause. I see the registrar is signalling to me.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, no, no. I just wanted to know what should be done with the various exhibits that were submitted by this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: May we briefly go into private session with respect to one of the documents that has been submitted, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Private session, and then we'll take a break until 4.45 and move to the next witness. All right. Let's go into a private session for a few minutes and then we'll take our break. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 5.33 p.m. to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 15th day of December, 1998 at 10.00 a.m.
